strengths: Addresses an important problem: relation hallucinations require reasoning beyond identifying objects. Combining subject–object–relation decomposition with accumulated textual and visual context is a plausible training-free approach.

Evaluates two model architectures on two relevant benchmarks and reports improvements over vanilla inference and two mitigation baselines. Reported accuracy gains over vanilla inference range from 4.81 to 7.56 percentage points.
Includes component ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, qualitative attention visualizations, and disclosure of approximately fourfold inference overhead.
weaknesses: The central results require reconciliation. Under standard binary precision and F1 definitions, Table 1 implies different ground-truth positive proportions for methods evaluated on the same benchmark. For example, LLaVA on MMRel implies approximately 50.7% positives for vanilla inference but 54.4% for ChainMPQ; on R-Bench, the corresponding values are 50.5% and 56.3%. These differences exceed rounding effects. No alternative metric aggregation or differing evaluation subsets are explained, undermining confidence in the comparisons.

Text-guided enhancement is technically underspecified. Equation 1 multiplies visual and textual features with separately defined dimensions without specifying an alignment projection. Its output is a convex combination of keyword embeddings, rather than an explicitly residual-enhanced visual representation. The paper does not explain how image information is preserved or how this operation is implemented within the distinct LLaVA and InstructBLIP pipelines.

The visual-memory equations contain a consequential inconsistency. In Equation 6, substituting alpha_j = lambda × confidence_j cancels lambda from the normalized weighted average, conflicting with its stated role as the memory-bias strength and the sensitivity analysis. Answer confidence is also undefined, and attention-head aggregation and the precise intervention locations are insufficiently specified.

Novelty and comparisons are insufficiently established. The method explicitly builds on interleaved-modal chain-of-thought but does not compare against ICoT or a compute-matched generic multistep reasoning baseline. The text-context ablation is useful, but reducing five questions to one confounds question design with inference budget. Stronger controls are needed to attribute improvements to the proposed decomposition and visual-memory mechanism.

Evaluation and reproducibility are limited. Only two older 7B models are tested, with no reported uncertainty, precise evaluation subset sizes, clear held-out hyperparameter selection protocol, or detailed decoding settings. Some improvements over the strongest baseline are small: 0.18 percentage points for LLaVA on R-Bench and 0.62 for InstructBLIP on MMRel. Their significance and the tradeoff against approximately fourfold inference cost remain unestablished.

Several conclusions exceed the evidence. Higher F1 does not establish preserved recall: the reported MMRel LLaVA metrics imply recall falling from approximately 84.0% for calibration to 79.1% for ChainMPQ. Selected attention maps do not establish reduced reliance on language priors or causal improvements in grounding, and no relation-category breakdown or systematic failure analysis supports the broader robustness claims.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: relational errors can persist even when a vision-language model recognizes the relevant objects correctly.
The training-free combination of question decomposition, textual context, and attention memory is intuitive and potentially useful.
Table 1 reports improvements across two model architectures and two relevant benchmarks. Component ablations and a hyperparameter sweep provide preliminary evidence beyond the main comparisons.
weaknesses: The central attention mechanism is technically underspecified. Equation 1 multiplies visual and textual features with potentially different dimensions without defining alignment projections. Its output consists of weighted combinations of keyword embeddings, rather than an explicit enhancement preserving visual features; no residual connection or integration procedure is specified. These omissions make the actual training-free implementation difficult to reconstruct.

The visual-memory equations contain consequential inconsistencies. Substituting α_j = λ·Conf_j into Equation 6 cancels λ entirely, leaving unclear how the reported λ sensitivity arises under that update. Answer confidence is undefined, and attention-head aggregation and the precise locations of attention interventions are unspecified. Applying the mechanism across LLaVA patch tokens and InstructBLIP's Q-Former representations requires substantially more explanation.

The reported metrics require clarification. Under standard binary precision/F1 definitions, Table 1's LLaVA MMRel results imply different positive-label prevalences for the same benchmark: approximately 50.7% for Vanilla versus 54.4% for ChainMPQ. The analogous R-Bench values are approximately 50.5% and 56.3%. These discrepancies exceed rounding error. If category averaging or different evaluated subsets explain them, the protocol must say so; otherwise the results are internally inconsistent. The claim of no recall sacrifice is also unsupported: the reported R-Bench precision/F1 values imply lower recall than Vanilla under standard definitions.

Novelty and attribution are insufficiently established. The method builds directly on interleaved multimodal reasoning, but does not compare against ICoT or straightforward multistep prompting under a matched inference budget. Removing four intermediate questions changes both decomposition and computation, so that ablation does not isolate the proposed question structure. Separate tests of confidence weighting, adaptive token selection, and accumulated versus last-step visual memory are missing.

The evaluation is too limited to substantiate broad effectiveness. Accuracy gains over the strongest baseline are only 0.18 percentage points on LLaVA/R-Bench and 0.62 points on InstructBLIP/MMRel, without uncertainty estimates or paired significance tests. Exact evaluated splits, sample counts, answer-parsing rules, and a separate hyperparameter-validation protocol are not provided. Evaluation covers only two older 7B models and lacks relation-category breakdowns, despite claims about spatial limitations.

The practical and grounding claims exceed the evidence. Appendix A.4 reports roughly fourfold inference time, but provides no controlled comparison of accuracy against computational cost. Selected attention visualizations do not establish faithful reasoning or reduced reliance on language priors. Moreover, questions that presuppose the queried relation can reinforce an incorrect premise; failure analysis and robustness tests are needed to assess this risk.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: relation hallucinations require reasoning beyond recognizing individual objects. The training-free combination of entity localization, complementary questions, and accumulated visual attention is practically motivated.

Table 1 reports improvements across both models and both benchmarks. Accuracy gains over the unmodified models range from 4.81 to 7.56 percentage points, with accompanying precision and F1 improvements.
Component ablations, hyperparameter analysis, qualitative examples, and an inference-cost estimate provide useful initial evidence about the framework.
weaknesses: The central evaluation needs clarification. Under standard binary classification definitions, Table 1's accuracy, precision, and F1 imply different ground-truth positive proportions for methods evaluated on the same benchmark. For example, LLaVA on R-Bench implies approximately 50.5% positives for Vanilla but 56.3% for ChainMPQ. This cannot be explained by rounding. Different aggregation conventions or evaluation subsets could explain it, but neither is specified; confusion matrices, exact splits, and metric definitions are needed to establish reliable comparisons.

The text-guided enhancement is not technically specified well enough to reproduce. Equation 1 multiplies visual and textual features with potentially different dimensions without defining alignment projections. Even with compatible dimensions, its output consists of mixtures of keyword embeddings, rather than retained visual features; no residual connection or integration mechanism explains how visual information is preserved. This is particularly consequential for a training-free method applied to two different architectures.

The attention-memory equations contain a substantive inconsistency. In Equation 6, normalizing by the sum of alpha values cancels the shared lambda factor, although the paper attributes its sensitivity results to lambda controlling historical attention strength. Confidence computation, attention-head aggregation, and the precise layers and positions receiving the bias are also unspecified. These gaps prevent verification of the proposed mechanism.

Comparisons do not adequately establish novelty or benefits beyond additional inference. The closely related ICoT method is discussed but not evaluated, and there are no compute-matched generic reasoning or repeated-question baselines. Removing multi-perspective questions also reduces the number of reasoning calls, confounding question design with computation. This matters because ChainMPQ costs approximately four times the base-model inference time, while some gains over the strongest baseline are only 0.18 or 0.62 accuracy points.

Evaluation breadth and reproducibility are insufficient for the generality claims. Experiments cover only two older 7B models, without stronger contemporary models, relation-category breakdowns, uncertainty estimates, or a clearly separate hyperparameter-validation split. Exact evaluated sample counts, decoding settings, and complete prompt-generation rules are missing. The stated relationship between kmax = 20 and 10% of visual tokens also requires architecture-specific explanation.

Several interpretations exceed the evidence. Higher precision and F1 do not establish preserved recall: under standard binary metrics, LLaVA's R-Bench recall decreases from approximately 96.9% to 93.9%. Two selected attention visualizations do not demonstrate suppression of language priors or causal grounding. Moreover, questions such as 'What is the dog chasing?' presuppose the queried relation and could reinforce false premises; systematic failure and error-propagation analyses are absent.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: relation hallucinations require reasoning about interactions beyond recognizing individual objects. Combining complementary questions with accumulated visual and textual context is a plausible training-free approach.
Table 1 reports consistent accuracy improvements across four LVLMs and two relation-focused benchmarks, including gains over constraint-aware prompting and Detect-then-Calibrate.
The paper includes component ablations, hyperparameter analysis, and latency measurements. The lightweight variants provide useful evidence about the accuracy–cost tradeoff.
weaknesses: The attention mechanism has unresolved mathematical problems. Equation 1 multiplies visual and textual features with potentially different dimensions without specifying projections or alignment. Its output is a mixture of keyword embeddings rather than preserved visual features; no residual connection or integration mechanism is described. More seriously, substituting α_j = λ·Conf_j into Equation 6 cancels λ entirely, including when only one previous mask exists. This conflicts with the reported sensitivity to λ and leaves the implemented algorithm unclear.

The main evaluation metrics require reconciliation. Under standard binary precision and F1 definitions, the MMRel accuracy/precision/F1 triples imply different ground-truth positive fractions for the same benchmark: approximately 50.7% for vanilla LLaVA, 54.4% for ChainMPQ on LLaVA, and 56.9% for ChainMPQ on InstructBLIP. These differences exceed rounding effects. If metrics use category averaging or different subsets, the aggregation and sampling protocols must be specified; otherwise, the central results are internally inconsistent.

Reproducibility is insufficient for the claimed architectural generality. The paper does not define the answer-confidence estimator, feature alignment, attention-head aggregation, or precise layers and token positions receiving the bias. The statement that 20 tokens represent 10% of visual patches is not reconciled with differing model tokenizations. Appendix A.3 additionally introduces GPT-3.5 Turbo for question refinement without its exact prompts, version, or generation settings.

The experimental comparisons do not adequately isolate the contribution from additional inference. The method uses five auxiliary questions and a final answer, but lacks a matched-compute repeated-reasoning baseline and direct comparison with the motivating ICoT approach or the discussed Triplet Description method. The text-only ablation is useful, but removing multi-perspective questions also reduces computation substantially. Confidence weighting and entropy-adaptive selection are not separately ablated.

Several improvements over the strongest baseline are small, including 0.18 percentage points on LLaVA R-Bench and 0.62 points on InstructBLIP MMRel, without confidence intervals or paired significance tests. Evaluation subset sizes, hyperparameter-selection splits, and relation-category breakdowns are insufficiently documented. Higher precision and F1 alone also do not establish the claimed absence of recall degradation.

The efficiency and broader-generalization claims remain incompletely supported. Full ChainMPQ increases reported latency from 0.9 to 3.3 seconds per sample, but hardware, decoding budgets, and inclusion of GPT-3.5 preprocessing costs are unspecified. The appendix does not explain how subject–object–relation decomposition applies to nonrelational MMBench/MME tasks, and switches from InternVL3.5 in the main experiments to InternVL3 in its tables. These gaps, together with the equation and metric inconsistencies, prevent the reported gains from constituting convincing acceptance-level evidence.

strengths: Addresses an important reliability problem: relation hallucinations in vision-language models. Combining entity localization, complementary questions, and accumulated visual attention is a plausible training-free approach.
Reports improvements across four model families and two relevant benchmarks. On MMRel, accuracy gains over the strongest compared baseline range from 0.62 to 2.16 percentage points.

Includes component ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity analysis, latency measurements, and reduced-cost variants. The visual-memory ablation provides some evidence that attention transfer contributes beyond textual context.
weaknesses: The central attention-enhancement operation is inadequately specified. Equation 1 multiplies visual and textual features with potentially different dimensions, without defining alignment projections. Its output is a weighted mixture of keyword embeddings, rather than preserved visual features; no residual connection or other mechanism explains how image information is retained. These omissions prevent faithful implementation across the four architectures.

The visual-memory equations contain a consequential inconsistency. In Equation 6, substituting α_j = λ·Conf_j causes the shared λ to cancel between numerator and denominator. This conflicts with the claimed control over bias strength and the λ sensitivity experiment. Confidence itself is undefined, and attention-head aggregation and the precise attention-modification locations are insufficiently specified.

The reported metrics require reconciliation. Under standard binary positive-class precision and F1, Table 1's MMRel accuracy/precision/F1 imply a positive-label prevalence of approximately 50.7% for vanilla LLaVA but 54.4% for ChainMPQ on the supposedly same dataset; the corresponding InstructBLIP figures are 50.6% and 56.9%. Rounding cannot explain these differences. If alternative averaging or different subsets were used, this must be stated. Consequently, confidence in the central evaluation is limited.

The comparisons do not sufficiently establish novelty or isolate the benefit of the proposed chain. ICoT is explicitly identified as an inspiration but is not compared experimentally, and the discussed Triplet Description method is also absent. There is no inference-budget-matched repeated-questioning or verification baseline. This matters because full ChainMPQ takes 3.3 seconds per sample versus 0.9 for vanilla inference.

Several improvements over competitive baselines are small, including 0.18 percentage points in LLaVA R-Bench accuracy and 0.01 points in InternVL MMRel F1. No uncertainty estimates or paired significance tests are provided. Ablations are restricted to one model and dataset, and do not separately validate adaptive token selection or confidence weighting. The claim that recall is preserved does not follow from increased F1; the reported LLaVA MMRel precision/F1 actually imply a slight recall decrease.

Reproducibility remains limited despite the appendix. GPT-3.5 Turbo is used to refine subquestions, but its prompts, version, generation settings, and inclusion in latency measurements are unspecified. Dataset splits, answer parsing, decoding settings, and hardware are not adequately documented. The assertion that 20 tokens represent 10% of visual patches is not explained across architectures with different visual-token counts.

The broader reasoning claims exceed the evidence. The appendix does not explain how the subject–object–relation pipeline handles nonrelational MMBench/MME questions, and switches from InternVL3.5 to InternVL3 without explanation. Qualitative attention maps establish neither causal grounding nor protection against error propagation; Figure 7 itself contains contradictory intermediate answers. Systematic failure analysis and results broken down by relation type are missing.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: relation hallucinations require reasoning about interactions beyond recognizing individual objects. Combining complementary questions with accumulated textual and visual context is a plausible approach.
Table 1 reports consistent accuracy improvements across four LVLMs and two relevant benchmarks, including stronger Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL3.5 models.
The paper includes component ablations, hyperparameter analysis, qualitative examples, and latency measurements. The lightweight variants provide useful evidence about the accuracy–latency tradeoff.
weaknesses: The main evaluation contains unresolved metric inconsistencies. Under standard binary precision and F1 definitions, the LLaVA R-Bench baseline implies approximately 50.5% positive examples, whereas ChainMPQ implies 56.3%, despite evaluation on the same dataset. These differences exceed rounding error. Any alternative averaging protocol must be specified; otherwise, the reported metrics cannot describe a consistent evaluation set. The same rows imply recall falling from approximately 96.9% to 93.9%, contradicting the claim that recall is not sacrificed.

The visual enhancement operation is inadequately specified. Equation 1 multiplies visual and text features with potentially different dimensions without defining alignment projections. Its output is a weighted combination of keyword embeddings, rather than an explicitly enhanced version of the original visual features. The paper does not explain residual connections, feature alignment, or integration into the four distinct architectures, making this central component difficult to reproduce or assess.

The attention-memory equations conflict with the hyperparameter interpretation. Substituting alpha_j = lambda times confidence_j into Equation 6 cancels the common lambda factor, so this aggregation does not provide the claimed control over bias strength. The relationship between Equations 5 and 6 needs clarification to explain the reported lambda sensitivity. Confidence computation, attention-head aggregation, and the precise attention entries modified are also unspecified.

Novelty and comparative evidence remain limited relative to the acknowledged ICoT inspiration. There is no direct ICoT comparison or comparison with the discussed triplet-description approach. Although the text-only ablation is useful, compute-matched multi-call reasoning or verification baselines would better establish whether the proposed visual-memory mechanism justifies its approximately 3.7-fold latency increase.

Several gains over the strongest baseline are modest, including 0.18 percentage points for LLaVA on R-Bench and 0.62 points for InstructBLIP on MMRel. No confidence intervals or paired significance analyses are supplied. Evaluation splits, hyperparameter-selection protocol, and results by relation category are insufficiently documented.

Reproducibility and broader claims need stronger support. Appendix A.3 introduces GPT-3.5 Turbo for question refinement without providing its exact prompts, version, or whether its cost is included in latency measurements. The appendix also does not explain how subject–object–relation decomposition applies to general MMBench/MME questions, and switches from InternVL3.5 to InternVL3 in its tables. These omissions weaken the claimed architectural generality and broader reasoning improvements.
